s1.syndrome_frame: Progressive vertigo with severe headaches and nausea, associated with a cerebellar mass
salient_findings: Severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting
Positive right-sided Dix-Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus
3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema
key_facts: 74-year-old man
History of metastatic prostate cancer
Known left upper lobe lung mass
Progressive vertigo over four weeks
Severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting
Positive for adenovirus
No focal motor or sensory deficits
Intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing
Intact gait despite dizziness
Positive right-sided Dix-Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus
3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema
Cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect

shortlist.label: Cerebellar metastasis from prostate cancer
shortlist.why_kept: History of metastatic prostate cancer and presence of a cerebellar mass

shortlist.label: Hemangioblastoma
shortlist.why_kept: Cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect, consistent with hemangioblastoma

shortlist.label: Cerebellar glioblastoma
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of a cerebellar mass with surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect

shortlist.label: Cerebellar astrocytoma
shortlist.why_kept: Cerebellar mass with cystic components, which can be seen in astrocytomas

shortlist.label: Medulloblastoma
shortlist.why_kept: Cerebellar mass in an adult, although less common, medulloblastoma is a consideration

raw.rationale: The patient has a history of metastatic prostate cancer and the presence of a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema, which is consistent with a metastatic lesion.

rejected.label: Hemangioblastoma
rejected.why: While considered, the patient's history of metastatic cancer makes a metastatic lesion more likely

rejected.label: Cerebellar glioblastoma
rejected.why: No evidence of a primary brain tumor and the patient's age and history suggest a metastatic lesion is more likely

rejected.label: Cerebellar astrocytoma
rejected.why: The patient's age and the presence of a cystic enhancing lesion are not typical for this diagnosis

rejected.label: Medulloblastoma
rejected.why: This is a rare tumor typically seen in children and young adults, making it an unlikely diagnosis for a 74-year-old man
